[Palacios-Prado and Bukauskas, Fig. 2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2736430/) · [Zonta et al., Fig. 1A–C](https://doi.org/10.1186/1478-811X-11-15)

claims.title: A blocked junction carries zero flux
claims.statement: Setting the effective transport scale to zero gives zero junction flux at every voltage and concentration difference.
assumptions: The constant-field route multiplies the concentration-dependent term by its effective area, permeability and opening scale.

numerical.result: The surface blocking and equilibrium tests passed on CPU.

biology.observable: Ion transfer rate attributable to a junction under a specified blocking condition, with the assay detection limit.
biology.finding: Heptanol suppressed junctional current in a bovine epithelial cell pair, and the current returned after washout. The trace has no reported detection threshold for residual ion flux. [Wang et al., Fig. 2E–F](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20089928/)

claims.title: Junction conductance relaxes toward a voltage-dependent target
claims.statement: At fixed voltage the intrinsic gate approaches its target with one exponential time constant and stays between its residual conductance fraction and one. Increasing voltage magnitude lowers the target if the residual fraction is below one. Reversing polarity preserves the trajectory from the same initial state.
assumptions: The junction has one intrinsic conductance state, the declared opening and closing rates, and a fixed threshold. Elapsed time is nonnegative and the initial conductance lies between the residual fraction and one.

The tissue applies an external availability multiplier to transport. The intrinsic gate keeps evolving during a block. The time-course identity assumes constant junction voltage throughout the interval.

numerical.result: Across 45 constant-voltage samples the compiled gate matched the independent reference within 1.12 × 10⁻¹⁶. In three tissue cell pairs the intrinsic gates continued moving during a 31.25 ms block, and tracer transfer after release matched the integrated reference within 8.68 × 10⁻¹⁸ fmol.

biology.observable: Normalized junction conductance at each clamp polarity and the number and duration of decay components during a fixed-voltage step.
biology.finding: Seven wild-type Cx43 cell pairs gave residual conductances of 0.35 ± 0.01 and 0.33 ± 0.01 relative to the prepulse at positive and negative voltages. At −100 mV the same decay had two time constants, 70 ± 5 and 931 ± 54 ms (SEM). The Cells reference parameters give one time constant of 50.0 ms. The experiment leaves exact transient polarity symmetry and the independent availability multiplier open. [Sahu and Bera, Table 2 and Fig. S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3607587/)

claims.title: Voltage-gated channel openings stay between zero and one
claims.statement: For the six Kv1 laws, Kir2.1 and NaV1.2, both targets lie between zero and one and both time constants are positive on the declared voltage interval. An exponential tissue stage preserves the opening bounds when its two endpoint voltages differ. At a fixed voltage each gate’s deviation from its target decays exponentially. The whole-current response combines both gates.
assumptions: Voltage is inside minus outside. Both stage endpoint voltages are between −120 and +60 mV, the elapsed time is nonnegative, and both initial gates lie in [0, 1].

The proof uses the declared kinetics and the tissue’s exponential stage in real arithmetic, including the small-step series and both branches of the regularized sodium rates. A whole-current trace at fixed voltage and concentrations is proportional to the open fraction.

numerical.result: The compiled dispatcher matched independent gate targets at 25 voltages within 2.23 × 10⁻¹⁶ and time constants within 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁵ s. All 72 stage cases stayed in [0, 1]. During the tissue block all eight gate pairs continued to move.

biology.observable: Normalized whole-current activation, decay or recovery for the same isoform, temperature, holding state and voltage-step sequence.
biology.finding: Rat Kv1.1 decay at −20 mV and 25 °C was 313 ± 82 ms (SD). Cells retained 88% of its peak after 1.5 s and gave a fit of about 8 s from an equilibrated −80 mV hold. Rat Kv1.4 retained under 2% after 3.2 s at 0 mV, versus 0.57% in Cells. Four gate parameters match that paper. Human NaV1.2 rose in 0.38 ± 0.05 ms (10–90%, SEM), versus 0.296 ms in Cells. Its fitted inactivation midpoint was −63.53 ± 0.79 mV, while Cells gave half of its −120 mV reference response at −54.9 mV. [Ranjan et al., Fig. 2C](https://doi.org/10.3389/fncel.2019.00358) · [Stühmer et al., Table I and Fig. 6](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1460-2075.1989.tb08483.x) · [Begemann et al., Table 2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s10020-019-0073-6)

claims.title: Channel opening scales the signed transfer of sodium or potassium
claims.statement: The seven gated K⁺ laws, one gated Na⁺ law and two single-ion leaks multiply the fully open constant-field flux by their opening and external availability. The opening is m h² for Kv1.1 and Kir2.1, m h for Kv1.2–Kv1.6, m³ h for NaV1.2 and one for the two leaks. With availability between zero and one the magnitude cannot exceed the fully open flux. Blocking gives zero. Only the declared ion crosses, debiting the cell and crediting the exterior.
assumptions: The declared population conducts K⁺ or Na⁺ with relative permeability one. The same area, permeability, abundance, voltage and concentrations define the fully open comparison. Positive flux points from the cell to the exterior.
The gate values and external availability are in [0, 1]. The formal booking uses one cell–exterior pair. A held bath offsets the exterior credit with reservoir supply.

numerical.result: All ten populations shared one membrane. Potassium moved out and sodium moved in after release. Every off-ion and padding transfer was zero. The largest per-channel cumulative discrepancy was 2.37 × 10⁻¹³ fmol against an independent adaptive solution.

biology.observable: Ion-specific flux or current at known driving force, with an independently measured availability or single-channel open fraction.
biology.unit: fmol/s or pA with the ion charge identified
biology.finding: At −60 mV, 100 µM cytoplasmic spermine reduced the Kir2.1 single-channel current magnitude from 2.00 ± 0.04 to 1.40 ± 0.04 pA with no significant change in open probability. A voltage-only gate misses that change in unitary conductance. The two generic leak laws have no assigned molecular isoform or preparation-specific permeability. [Xie et al., Figs. 1–3](https://doi.org/10.1085/jgp.20028576)

claims.title: Chloride gradients set leak reversal and inward chloride carries positive outward current
claims.statement: For the gate-free Cl⁻ population, outward material flux J produces outward electrical current −F × 10⁻¹⁵ × J amperes for J in fmol/s. The conducting route reverses at V = (RT/F) × (ln inside − ln outside) on the regular Bernoulli branch and at zero voltage. On the small nonzero branch its reversal follows the implemented polynomial ratio.
assumptions: Voltage is inside minus outside. Concentrations, absolute temperature, F and RT are positive. Permeability, area, abundance and availability give a positive scale for the reversal claim.

The formal calculation is over real numbers. The regular branch uses |FV/(RT)| ≥ 10⁻⁴. The sign conversion applies to either flux branch. In the tissue comparison, a single membrane connects the cell to a grounded bath and the chloride population is the only conductive route.

numerical.result: At the same initial voltage, 147 and 70 mM bath chloride gave opposite fluxes and initial electrode currents of +0.573 and −5.733 pA. The two tissue trajectories matched an independent solution within 1.58 × 10⁻¹² fmol of transfer, with zero off-ion and padding flux.

biology.observable: Shift in the single-channel reversal potential when the nominal extracellular chloride concentration changes at fixed intracellular chloride and temperature.

evidence.locator: Figure 1B and accompanying Results.
evidence.context: Cell-attached apical patches of cultured rabbit collecting-tubule principal cells at 37 °C. Pipette chloride was lowered from 145 to 15 mM by partial substitution with gluconate. The voltage scale is relative to the resting membrane potential.
evidence.uncertainty: The two conditions used 11 and 4 patches, with no endpoint uncertainty reported.
evidence.assessment: The measured shift is approximate. Lowering nominal outside chloride from 145 to 15 mM in rabbit kidney patches at 37 °C shifted reversal in the predicted positive direction. The channels also passed bromide and showed regulated opening. Absolute permeability remains uncalibrated.

claims.title: Passive neutral solute follows its concentration gradient
claims.statement: For a neutral solute the inward constant-field flux is the route scale times outside minus inside concentration at any voltage. With a positive scale it is inward exactly when concentration is higher outside. In a closed pair the gradient changes at rate −k times the gradient, where k is the scale times the sum of the reciprocal compartment volumes.
assumptions: Valence is zero. The route scale is area × permeability × opening divided by mol/fmol. Concentrations are in mM and flux is in fmol/s.
The relaxation identity applies to two well-mixed compartments at fixed positive volumes in pL, with this route as the sole transfer of the solute.

numerical.result: Five compiled cases agreed with the independent flux within 7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ fmol/s. In the closed tissue pair at 20 ms, the largest relative error in final compartment amount was 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ against a 5 × 10⁻⁴ tolerance.

biology.observable: Signed passive transfer rate of an identified neutral solute at measured free concentrations on both sides, with compartment volumes or measured flux per area and the corresponding area.
biology.finding: Urea flux was measured over time in liposomes of three lipid compositions. Comparing a Cells rate requires the gradient, area and permeability for the same preparation. [Lande et al., Fig. 3](https://doi.org/10.1085/jgp.106.1.67)

claims.title: Ion charge sets permeation reversal and bounds the current–voltage slope
claims.statement: For a passive ion of either sign, the analytic flux reverses at its Nernst voltage and dissipates nonnegative heat. At fixed concentrations the electrical slope conductance stays between the lower and higher concentrations multiplied by the same positive factor. Equal concentrations give a linear current–voltage relation.
assumptions: Temperature, concentrations and compartment volumes are positive. The reversal requires nonzero ion charge and positive permeability, area and opening. The conductance bound also includes a closed route.

Conductance holds at fixed concentrations, permeability and opening. In the engine’s real-arithmetic evaluator the slope bounds exclude the two switches at |zFV/(RT)| = 0.0001. The secant bound assumes the whole voltage interval stays within one branch. The material response holds at fixed volumes and voltage.

The biological current predictions assume the same effective permeability at both voltages within each preparation. A red-cell current is inferred from net solute transfer, and a planar-bilayer current is measured under voltage clamp.

numerical.result: 360 CPU float64 component cases matched high-precision flux, heat and slope references. In two finite tissue pairs, halving the step from 64 to 128 steps reduced errors in signed transfer, heat and final voltage by factors of 4.03–4.05. Both amount ledgers matched the transferred material.

biology.observable: Electrical current at a second voltage and reversal at a known ion gradient. These experiments leave microscopic route heat unmeasured.
biology.unit: mA per g Hb (red cells), nA (bilayer) and mV (reversal)

evidence.citation: Freedman and Novak, Figs. 5–6 and Table I
evidence.locator: The lower Fig. 6A points give chloride currents. Fig. 6C gives measured voltages at the two external potassium concentrations. Fig. 5 gives conductances.
evidence.context: DIDS-treated human red cells, five donor series at 23 °C and pH 7.5. Optical shrinkage estimates net chloride transfer. A parallel pH assay estimates membrane voltage.
evidence.uncertainty: Means and SD were digitized. Estimated figure-reading precision is ±1.5 mV and ±0.05 mA/g Hb. The within-donor covariance is unavailable.
evidence.assessment: At −59 mV, the one-voltage fit predicted −1.97 mA/g Hb against −1.17 ± 0.13 measured. The ratio of reported mean slope conductances was 3.67. At the inferred fixed chloride concentrations the model permits a local slope ratio up to 1.49.

evidence.locator: Open magenta squares for asymmetric KCl at matched light state. The text reports the interpolated reversal.
evidence.context: Planar bilayer under voltage clamp with a 150/15 mM potassium gradient and valinomycin. The comparison assumes 25 °C.
evidence.uncertainty: The plotted currents are readable to about ±1 nA. The panel gives no pointwise uncertainties or measurement temperature. The reversal is interpolated from the same curve.
evidence.assessment: The predicted reversal was −59.16 mV against −59.8 mV measured. At −110 mV the same fitted permeability gave −3.84 nA against approximately −13.5 nA measured.

claims.title: Voltage and free proton concentrations set the leak reversal
claims.statement: For an open route, inward flux is positive exactly when hOut exceeds hIn × B(−x)/B(x), using the engine’s selected Bernoulli factor at x = FV/(RT). The analytic law reverses at V = (RT/F) × (ln hOut − ln hIn) and releases nonnegative instantaneous heat. The engine’s real-arithmetic evaluator gives the analytic flux at x = 0 and for |x| ≥ 10⁻⁴. At other x the polynomial has its own reversal ratio.
assumptions: Positive free H⁺ concentrations on both sides in mM, positive absolute temperature and proton valence +1. Voltage is inside minus outside, with positive flux inward.
Area × permeability × opening is positive for directional claims and may be zero for the heat inequality. The proof interprets both evaluator branches in real arithmetic.

numerical.result: Twelve compiled CPU cases agreed with the 70-digit flux reference within 1.55 × 10⁻²⁰ fmol/s. In a buffered tissue cell, using free H⁺ gave the observed inward rate of 3.31 × 10⁻⁶ fmol/s. Substituting total intracellular proton equivalents reversed the predicted direction.

biology.observable: Reversal voltage of an open H⁺ path across measured pH gradients at known temperature. Predicting the signed flux magnitude also requires permeability, area and opening.
biology.finding: In Jurkat T cells the proton-current reversal shifted −47 mV per pH unit, versus an ideal −58 mV per pH unit. The fitted slope uncertainty and intracellular pH limit a quantitative verdict. [Schilling et al., Fig. 2E](https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.2002.028878)
biology.unit: mV at reversal, fmol/s for signed proton flux

claims.title: Free energy sets ATP-driven transport direction and stall
claims.statement: With positive forward rate J⁺, an enabled cycle has net rate J⁺(1 − exp(ΔG/RT)). It runs forward for negative ΔG, reverses for positive ΔG and stalls at zero. A disabled cycle has zero rate. Instantaneous heat is nonnegative in every case. For n protons per ATP, the stall voltage is (RT/F) ln(a_P/a_N) + ΔG_fuel/(nF). Neutral cargo flux is independent of voltage at fixed activities and forward rate.
assumptions: One tightly coupled mode hydrolyses one ATP on side N and moves n cargo units from N to P. Cargo valence is +1 for free protons and zero for the neutral role. Voltage is V_N − V_P.

Activities and absolute temperature are positive. In an enabled population, capacity, availability and the saturation factor are positive. Lean represents their product by its finite logarithm and uses real arithmetic.

numerical.result: Across 92 compiled tissue states, 72 ran forward, 16 reversed and four were within the stall tolerance. Cycle flux agreed with frozen references to 7.50 × 10⁻¹⁶ fmol/s and heat was nonnegative in all cases. Offsetting the voltage by ±10 mV about proton stall reversed the rate. The same voltage perturbations preserved all three flowing neutral controls. Eight capacity and availability controls gave exactly zero flux, heat and work.

biology.observable: Reversal voltage of ATP-dependent proton transport at known fuel and proton activities, and neutral-cargo flux at fixed activities under varied voltage.
biology.finding: In yeast vacuoles at cytosolic pH 8.5 and vacuolar pH 5.0, measured reversal was −17.5 ± 5 mV (SE, six trials). The tightly coupled two-proton prediction was −86.5 mV. The authors proposed a proton shunt. Vesicles showed ATP-dependent riboflavin uptake. Neutral-cargo reversal and voltage independence remain open. [Kettner et al., Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1303676/) · [Van Herwaarden et al., Fig. 3E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1800714/)
biology.unit: mV for reversal, fmol/s for signed cargo flux

claims.title: Stall voltages and net charge of the sodium–potassium and calcium pumps
claims.statement: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stalls at ψ = g_NaK − 3r_Na + 2r_K and the calcium pump at ψ = (g_Ca − r_Ca)/2. An enabled pump runs forward above its own stall voltage. Their outward charge flux in elementary-charge equivalents is J_NaK + 2J_Ca. The same sum determines their voltage-dependent free-energy change. The two currents cancel exactly when J_NaK = −2J_Ca.
assumptions: For each ion, r is ln(inside activity / outside activity), ψ = F(V_inside − V_outside)/(RT), and each g is its pump’s ATP hydrolysis free energy divided by RT. Temperature and all activities are positive. The direction and stall results assume positive capacity, availability and saturation.

J denotes signed cycles per unit time. Each forward cycle consumes one ATP. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump exports three Na⁺ and imports two K⁺. The Cells calcium pump transports one Ca²⁺ outward and counts only that ion. The formula sums the currents of these two pumps.

numerical.result: The compiled tissue matched two 80-digit references at five initial voltages, including both stalls (−99.365 and −104.104 mV). The largest cycle-rate error was 3.50 × 10⁻¹⁶ fmol/s. At the midpoint the pumps ran in opposite directions, each contributing 0.349 pA in magnitude. The net electrode current was 2.04 × 10⁻²⁶ A. The 1 ms trajectory accounted for all three ions and both midpoint pumps dissipated energy.

biology.observable: Ion transfer per ATP, paired ion flux and outward current, and stall voltage under known fuel and ion activities.
biology.finding: Squid axons gave 3.05 ± 0.13 Na⁺ per net charge from −60 to −90 mV in Na-free seawater and 2.72 ± 0.09 at 0 mV with 390 mM external Na⁺ (SEM). Cells predicts 3. Red-cell ghosts lost about 3 Na⁺ per ATP. In pig-brain calcium pumps, separate rate measurements imply 1.02 Ca²⁺ per ATP and about +1.4 net charges per ATP after inward H⁺ is included. Cells counts +2 from Ca²⁺ alone. The simulated stall voltages still lack a matched measurement. [Rakowski et al., Table I](https://doi.org/10.1085/jgp.93.5.903) · [Garrahan and Glynn](https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.1967.sp008297) · [Salvador et al., Table I](https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.29.18230)
biology.unit: ions per net elementary charge, ions and net elementary charges per ATP, mV for stall

claims.title: Extracellular face flux follows the electrochemical potential drop
claims.statement: Reversing the endpoints and voltage reverses the signed flux. A positive face coefficient gives positive flux exactly when the sender’s electrochemical potential is higher. At equilibrium the flux is zero, including when the concentration and electrical drives cancel.
assumptions: Both endpoint concentrations and RT are positive. The two orientations use the same ion, temperature, geometry and diffusivity.
The proof evaluates the two log-ratio branches and the fourth-degree small-gradient mean in exact real arithmetic. The force uses the difference of the endpoint logs.

numerical.result: Opposing voltage reversed a resolved concentration-driven flux. At zero voltage, 100.00000000000001 and 100 mM gave zero CPU flux versus 1.42 × 10⁻¹⁸ fmol/s in the scalar reference. The absolute tolerance was 3 × 10⁻¹² fmol/s. Across 60 tissue flux observations, the largest absolute discrepancy was 1.50 × 10⁻¹⁷ fmol/s.

biology.observable: Species-resolved ion transfer rate between two extracellular compartments, with measured concentrations at both endpoints and their voltage difference.
biology.finding: Diluting NaCl on opposite sides of a claudin-2 pore shifted its current-reversal voltage in opposite directions. Reversal of an individual ion’s net flux remains unmeasured. [Weber et al., Fig. 6A–B](https://elifesciences.org/articles/09906)

claims.title: Passive extracellular face transport dissipates energy
claims.statement: Each ion’s signed flux multiplied by its electrochemical potential drop is nonnegative. Summing the contributions over all ions gives nonnegative instantaneous face power.
assumptions: Endpoint concentrations and RT are positive. Each ion has a nonnegative face coefficient. Power is evaluated at a single state.

numerical.result: Face power agreed with the scalar reference across eleven CPU cases. Reversing a resolved flux and its endpoint bookings preserved the total material rate and gave −4.52 × 10⁻⁵ pJ/s, failing the direction and power checks.

biology.observable: Instantaneous energy loss inferred from species-resolved fluxes and measured electrochemical potential differences across an extracellular interface.
biology.finding: Trout gill epithelia supplied two-way sodium tracer flux and voltage measurements. Active transport contributed to the measured flux, so passive heat production cannot be inferred from these data alone. [Galvez et al., Fig. 3 and Tables 1–2](https://www.zoology.ubc.ca/~woodcm/Woodblog/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/Galvez-et-al.-2008-In-Vitro-Cell.pdf)

claims.title: Edge orientation preserves each compartment’s transfer balance
claims.statement: Reversing any subset of edge orientations and their signed fluxes preserves each compartment’s credit or debit.
assumptions: Every transfer is booked once at its sender and once at its receiver. The edge set is finite and multiple edges may share a compartment.

numerical.result: The per-cell comparison passed for the declared owners. Swapping owners alone preserved the global total and produced a per-cell discrepancy of 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ fmol/s.

biology.observable: Net ion gain or loss in each of two identified compartments over the same transfer interval.
biology.finding: Paired clamp recordings showed equal and opposite junctional currents. Calibrated gain and loss of the same ion in both cells remain unmeasured. [Wang and Veenstra, Fig. 1A and C](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9101407/)

claims.title: Only boundary transfers change a region’s inventory during transport
claims.statement: Internal edges cancel when transfers are summed over a region. On the entire closed graph each species and any charge-weighted sum are conserved.
assumptions: Each edge transfers equal amounts between its two endpoints. A held bath needs an external supply term when included in an inventory.

numerical.result: The closed tissue run checked the potassium ledger, including membrane, pump and channel contributions. The chain comparison exercised both entering and leaving transfers on a four-compartment region.

biology.observable: Change in regional ion amount and net ion transfer across its boundary over the same interval.
biology.finding: Perfused rat hearts lost 139 ± 12 μmol of K⁺ per g dry weight in effluent over 40 min. Tissue depletion was measured in separate hearts, leaving the within-heart balance open. [Kuki et al., Figs. 3–4](https://doi.org/10.1161/01.RES.67.2.401)

claims.title: Balanced reactions preserve a weighted inventory
claims.statement: If each reaction balances an integer-weighted inventory, the combined update preserves that inventory for any signed real reaction extents.
assumptions: The species and reaction sets at the site are finite. Each species change equals its signed stoichiometric coefficients times the extents, summed over reactions.

numerical.result: The enzyme example compared four stored species changes with the declared coefficients and two nonzero extents across one CPU half-step.

biology.observable: Amount of a specified conserved chemical group across all its species at a closed site.
biology.finding: The measured G6P + F6P pool fell 0.613357 mM (7.31%) in the first of five time courses. The raw acquisition lists 0.950 mL and different timing from the workbook. Volumes, shared calibration and unobserved pools limit the amount balance. [Eicher et al., Fig. 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-1989/2/4/818) · [Publisher’s workbook](https://mdpi-res.com/metabolites/metabolites-02-00818/article_deploy/metabolites-02-00818-s001.zip)
biology.unit: fmol for the target inventory, mM for the measured soluble pool

claims.title: Binding and catalysis conserve enzyme and substrate
claims.statement: In E + S ⇌ C and C → E + P, total enzyme is E + C and total substrate is S + C + P. Omitting the returned E loses one enzyme unit per catalytic event while preserving substrate.
assumptions: Each complex carries one enzyme unit and one substrate unit. Each product retains one substrate unit. The site has no external supply or removal.

numerical.result: Lean checked both fixture columns and both weight rows. The largest absolute inventory residual in the CPU half-step was about 1.12 × 10⁻²⁰ fmol, below the 6.94 × 10⁻¹⁸ fmol tolerance. The engine refused the missing-enzyme reaction.

biology.observable: Free enzyme, substrate, bound complex and product amounts in a specified closed enzyme preparation.
biology.finding: NMR resolved ligand states bound to triosephosphate isomerase. Testing both balances requires simultaneous amounts of free enzyme, substrate, bound complex and product during turnover. [Rozovsky and McDermott, Figs. 3–5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1794347/)

claims.title: One-site binding follows the free ligand concentration
claims.statement: At equilibrium the occupied fraction of sites is c / (Kd + c), where c is free ligand concentration and Kd is the dissociation constant. The normalized weights of the two binder forms give the same fraction.
assumptions: One ligand binds one site. Each binder has a free and a singly occupied form, with positive total sites and positive association and dissociation rates. Kd is their off-rate divided by their on-rate.
Both concentrations are expressed in mM. The rate-balance theorem allows zero free ligand. The log-weight theorem uses positive free ligand and a positive Kd.

numerical.result: Across thirteen manufactured S1 states, the largest absolute occupancy difference from the independent reference was 3.33 × 10⁻¹⁶. Using total ligand in the same formula failed all thirteen. The first state also passed through the tissue’s stage read.

biology.observable: Equilibrium bound fraction across a free ligand titration at specified temperature and solution conditions.
biology.finding: For oxygen binding to human myoglobin at 10 °C, two digitized points set the affinity. The other three gave a root-mean-square error of 0.0422 in fractional occupancy. All five come from one figure with unknown pointwise uncertainty. [Rossi-Fanelli and Antonini, Fig. 2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13584010/) · [Digitized points](https://bi1.caltech.edu/2017/code/t05_nonlinear_regression.html)

claims.title: Uncharged membrane insertion dissipates nonnegative capacitor heat
claims.statement: The exact network heat in pJ is (10¹²/2) times the sum of C(ΔV)² + ΔC(V + ΔV)² over patches and every allocated patch share is nonnegative. For a single patch against a held bath, the heat is (10¹²/2) C V² ΔC/(C + ΔC) and the bath supplies zero image charge during insertion.
assumptions: Inserted membrane arrives uncharged. Each free node keeps its charge and each held node keeps its potential. The network is finite and the voltage changes obey its capacitor equations.
C and ΔC are nonnegative, expressed in F, with positive starting C in the one-patch formula. V and ΔV are in volts. The proof uses real arithmetic.

numerical.result: Both versions passed six control half-steps each. At an extreme ΔC/C of 1.7 × 10¹⁶, both computed −0.043037 pJ against an 80-digit reference of +0.051603 pJ and refused step one. The computed bath image charge was −3.638 × 10⁻¹² C. Using the sum-of-squares heat and exact single-patch image charge in a diagnostic control allowed both runs to finish. The lead confirmed the step refusal and assigned the fix to the operators owner.

biology.observable: Membrane capacitance, patch voltage and clamp charge during a characterized insertion event, with the incoming membrane’s initial charge accounted for.
biology.finding: Capacitance steps were measured during secretion in chromaffin cells. Testing insertion heat also needs the initial charge of the added membrane and independent electrical work and energy measurements. [Neher and Marty](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.79.21.6712)
biology.unit: pJ for heat, C for image charge

claims.title: Molecule entry scales with reservoir activity and assembly size, and exit with species count
claims.statement: For species i, each molecule in an assembly adds kᵢ to its exit rate. Entry occurs at kᵢθᵢN, where θᵢ = Kᵢρᵢ and N is total size. Balancing every species’ entry and exit at a nonempty state requires Σθᵢ = 1. With a common positive leave constant, the mean-field fractions are stationary at xᵢ = θᵢ/Σθⱼ during growth. Unequal leave constants can move the fractions away from those proportions.
assumptions: The well-mixed assembly has finitely many species with integer counts. The transfer constants Kᵢ, held activities ρᵢ and leave constants kᵢ are positive. Exchange has no catalytic multiplier and time is nominal.
A species’ instantaneous net rate is its entry rate minus its exit rate at the same state. The mean-field fraction derivative uses these rates for the count derivatives and requires N > 0.

numerical.result: Compiled rates agreed with rational reference values across all 165 three-species compositions through size eight. Doubling one species’ held activity doubled its entry and preserved the other rates. At equal counts (1, 1) and θ = (1, 1), the first fraction’s mean-field derivative was zero with leave constants (1, 1) and −¼ per nominal time unit with (1, 2).

biology.observable: Loss of accessible lipid during washout and uptake of a specified lipid as free monomer activity and individual vesicle size vary.
biology.unit: s⁻¹ for washout, M⁻¹ s⁻¹ per molar vesicles for the insertion constant
biology.finding: Accessible fluorescent lipid washed out of 310 protein-free vesicles at 0.0108 ± 0.0045 s⁻¹ (24 °C, mean ± SD). The retained fraction was 49.5 ± 8.5%. In a separate sterol assay, adding more equal-sized vesicles increased transfer at 25 °C. The insertion constant fitted at 35 °C was (6.4 ± 0.6) × 10⁷ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ per molar vesicles. Individual vesicle size, free monomer activity and the Cells time scale remain open. [Veit et al., Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41594-026-01821-8) · [Estronca et al., Fig. 2 and Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2098731/)

claims.title: Single-molecule exchange heat equals the change in assembly log weight
claims.statement: For entry between two nonempty compositions, the logarithm of the entry rate divided by the reverse exit rate at arrival equals the change in the assembly’s log weight. Reversing the event reverses the heat. At extinction the engine assigns the empty state log weight zero, so the last molecule of type i books −ln θᵢ.
assumptions: The uncatalyzed assembly exchanges one molecule at a time with positive activities and rate constants. For N > 0 the composition weight is (N−1)! times the product of θᵢ^(nᵢ)/nᵢ! over all species, where θᵢ = Kᵢρᵢ.
The empty state has zero entry propensity. Its terminal booking uses the change in log weight. The theorem concerns individual transfers in exact arithmetic.

numerical.result: Across 357 reversible pairs the largest difference from the independent log-weight change was 4.53 × 10⁻¹⁶ kBT. Two seeded lineages exercised three divisions and a terminal exit. Their saved log weight, heat, fission work and discarded free energy agreed with the independent calculation within 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁵ kBT.

biology.observable: Single-molecule entry and reverse exit rates at known neighboring compositions, with an independent transfer free-energy difference under the same conditions.

claims.title: Pair-consistent catalysis preserves the heat of a reversible transfer
claims.statement: A molecule entering an assembly sees the same catalytic multiplier as its reverse exit when the moving molecule is excluded from both catalyst counts. The log ratio of the two rates then equals the base exchange log-weight change. A singleton’s exit has multiplier one.
assumptions: The species set is finite. The counts are nonnegative integers and the catalytic matrix β has nonnegative entries. The assembly exchanges one molecule at a time, with positive rate and transfer constants and fixed positive reservoir activities.
The reversible transfer connects two nonempty compositions. The singleton’s exit into the empty state is a separate boundary case. Lean evaluates the sums in exact arithmetic.

numerical.result: The 210 ordinary transfer pairs agreed with the base heat within 5.00 × 10⁻¹⁶ kBT. Two admitted one-event runs with a large diagonal coefficient lost the remaining catalyst in the reverse sum. The passive ledger refused both, booking 2.33 × 10⁻¹⁰ and 0.693147 kBT where the exact heat is zero. Both one-event controls passed. The lead accepted these false refusals and assigned the repair to the builder after its current test run. The recorded failure applies to the pinned engine revision.

biology.observable: Entry, reverse exit and independent affinity for the same lipid as the surrounding membrane composition changes.
biology.unit: M⁻¹ s⁻¹ per molar vesicles for entry, s⁻¹ for exit
biology.finding: For the same lipid tracer at 308 K, changing pure POPC vesicles to 1:1 POPC/cholesterol halved the fitted entry constant. Exit estimates were 25 ± 2 and 27 ± 2 s⁻¹. Independent titrations gave association constants of 1.3 × 10⁹ and 6.1 × 10⁸ M⁻¹. A shared catalytic multiplier at fixed affinity cannot explain the change. The fit used the equilibrium measurement, and molecular neighbor counts remain unknown. [Sampaio et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1529/biophysj.104.054007)

claims.title: Single-event catalysis can give different forward and reverse cycle rate products
claims.statement: The single-event rule evaluates the moving species’ multiplier at each event’s departure state. This adds the log ratio of two composition-dependent multipliers to the base heat. A rank-one β with only β_AA = 1 gives a four-transfer cycle ratio of 81/80. If adding one to every entry of β gives a positive rank-one matrix, the extra heat is a difference of state values and sums to zero around closed paths.
assumptions: The assembly exchanges with a held reservoir and each reversible edge joins nonempty states. Base propensities and multipliers are positive on the edges in the cycle.

The explicit square starts with one molecule each of A and B and follows +A, +B, −A, −B. The sufficient rank-one condition is 1 + βᵢⱼ = uᵢvⱼ. Then the correction to the base log weight is −ln(Σⱼ vⱼnⱼ / N).

numerical.result: The CPU agreed with rational forward and reverse rate products on 81 four-step cycles across three matrices. The rank-one β example gave 81/80. With a rank-one entrywise shift, all 27 cycles had ratio one in the exact reference and all 70 CPU edges matched the corrected log weight within 4.45 × 10⁻¹⁶ kBT. The lead corrected the design and assigned the matching code wording to the builder. [Design correction](https://github.com/Eidosoma/Cells/blob/0b564f2d99f70995c741456d7f55a515d049dd4d/docs/GARD_DESIGN.md#L320)

biology.observable: Forward and reverse transition rates around the same four known lipid compositions under a fixed reservoir, including the identity of the moving lipid.

claims.title: Whole-molecule counts set the ideal mixing cost of membrane entry
claims.statement: For a membrane with N molecules and a molecules of the incoming species, the activity for adding one molecule relative to its standard state is (a + 1)/(N + 1 − c). A finite source pool also contributes its count and standard concentration to the transfer energy.
assumptions: The ideal term uses log factorials of integer counts. The measure offset c is 0 or 1. For N ≥ c the activity formula applies directly. The first insertion into an empty membrane has only the entering species’ standard energy.
The equilibrium experiment measures bulk activity relative to cholesterol crystals. The ideal bulk curve is A = s x with one fitted reference-state scale s and cholesterol mole fraction x.

numerical.result: Both registered measures agreed with exact-factorial state weights on 592 compositions in the ideal-only world, within 2.14 × 10⁻¹⁴ kBT. Reference rates and independent ledger replay passed. At equal A and B counts with N = 6 the insertion activities were 4/7 and 4/6.

biology.observable: Equilibrium cholesterol activity as a function of membrane mole fraction.
biology.unit: dimensionless activity relative to crystalline cholesterol

evidence.citation: Shaw et al. (2023), Fig. 2A and Table S1
evidence.locator: Table S1, printed page 13, gives the 25 DOPC readings and both 68% confidence half-widths.
evidence.context: Protein-free DOPC/cholesterol large unilamellar vesicles equilibrated with methyl-beta-cyclodextrin at room temperature. Activity 1 refers to crystalline cholesterol.
evaluation: Hold out each of the 23 distinct composition values printed in Table S1, keeping rows with the same value together.
evidence.uncertainty: Activity and mole fraction come from the same fit and share a calibration across samples. The published marginal intervals omit their covariance. The comparison also reports sensitivity to weighting by both intervals.
evidence.assessment: Holding out each composition in turn gave a root-mean-square activity error of 0.0953. At 45.6 mol% the ideal prediction was 0.791 and the measured activity was 0.45 ± 0.02. This bulk series leaves the finite-count convention open.

evidence.locator: Figure 3 and its accompanying microscopy results give a crystal-onset mole fraction of 0.66 ± 0.02 across three series.
evidence.context: Optical microscopy detected cholesterol monohydrate in hydrated DOPC/cholesterol samples. The microscopy equilibration and stage temperatures are unspecified.
fit: Shaw Table S1 DOPC activity curve
evidence.uncertainty: The ±0.02 in composition has no stated confidence level. At equilibrium with the same solid chemical potential, onset corresponds to activity 1. Shaw did not characterize its crystal polymorph.
evidence.assessment: Extrapolating from the highest fitted composition (45.6 mol%) to the independently measured crystal onset (66 ± 2 mol%) gives activity 1.119. The expected value is 1 if the crystal references match.

claims.title: Pair interactions change the energy of membrane entry with composition
claims.statement: Updating the symmetric pair energy equals recomputing it from all membrane counts. For A entering a binary membrane with b molecules of B and total N, the excess insertion energy is χb²/[N(N + 1)] and the bulk excess chemical potential is χ(b/N)².
assumptions: The pair matrix is symmetric and counts remain in their physical domain. For the binary result the diagonal is zero, χ is the unlike-pair energy in kBT and N is positive.

The bulk comparison treats the cholesterol/DOPC membrane as a homogeneous binary mixture at fixed temperature. It uses one composition-independent χ and a fitted scale for the cholesterol crystal reference.

numerical.result: Under both measures, the signed pair matrix matched the reference energy within 2.14 × 10⁻¹⁴ kBT. The reversible edge identities passed. With equal counts and χ = 1, adding A cost an extra 0.214286 kBT at N = 6 and 0.245902 at N = 60.

biology.observable: Equilibrium cholesterol activity as a function of membrane mole fraction under a binary interaction model.
biology.unit: dimensionless activity relative to crystalline cholesterol

evidence.locator: Table S1, printed page 13, gives the 25 DOPC readings and both 68% confidence half-widths.
evidence.context: Protein-free DOPC/cholesterol large unilamellar vesicles equilibrated with methyl-beta-cyclodextrin at room temperature. Activity 1 refers to crystalline cholesterol.
evaluation: Hold out each of the 23 distinct composition values printed in Table S1, keeping rows with the same value together.

evidence.assessment: The interaction term lowered the held-composition activity error from 0.0953 to 0.0782. At 45.6 mol% it predicted 0.677 against 0.45 ± 0.02. Weighting by both measured uncertainties shifted the fitted interaction from 0.75 to 1.02 kBT.

evidence.locator: Figure 3 and its accompanying microscopy results give a crystal-onset mole fraction of 0.66 ± 0.02 across three series.
evidence.context: Optical microscopy detected cholesterol monohydrate in hydrated DOPC/cholesterol samples. The microscopy equilibration and stage temperatures are unspecified.
fit: Shaw Table S1 DOPC activity curve
evidence.uncertainty: The ±0.02 in composition has no stated confidence level. At equilibrium with the same solid chemical potential, onset corresponds to activity 1. Shaw did not characterize its crystal polymorph.
evidence.assessment: Extrapolating from 45.6 mol% to the independently measured crystal onset (66 ± 2 mol%) gives activity 0.804. The ideal prediction, 1.119, is closer to the expected activity of 1 if the crystal references match.

claims.title: Finite molecule counts set stochastic encounter rates and paired event heat
claims.statement: A molecular encounter draws from the available counts without replacement. For a regular, finite two-way edge with a common locus extent and catalyst factor, log(forward rate / reverse rate) equals minus the free-energy change plus held-reservoir work. At full membrane consumption the declared cancellation determines the boundary rate.
assumptions: Counts and reaction coefficients are natural numbers. The engine admits at most three reactants or products per side. The factorial identity holds for any finite integer order.

For the regular pair identity the residual membrane count after drawing all reactants is at least the measure offset. At offset one, full consumption without a shared participant uses the cancelled denominator. Overlap at full order can give a singular rate. The kept, extinct and reversible tokens govern which boundary events can fire.
The occupancy specialization uses one R molecule, distinct G partners, an ideal dilute pool and two reversible states at fixed volume.

numerical.result: The reference and engine agreed on ordinary rates and zero and singular patterns across 594 compositions under both count measures. Three boundary conventions were checked on six additional states. The pool kernel reproduced the two-state occupancy formula at one, two and three partners.

biology.observable: Bound probability for one molecule as the integer count of its distinct partner changes, and association events for identical reactants at known counts.
biology.finding: For identical membrane partners, live-cell homodimer imaging measured a 91 ± 16 ms lifetime. It reported surface densities, leaving the repeated-reactant draw at fixed small counts open. [Kasai et al., Figs. 4–6](https://doi.org/10.1083/jcb.201009128)

evidence.locator: Experimental grey bars for one dimer in the three classes with one red strand, at 250 nm radius. Table 1 and Fig. S8 provide the kinetic and independent bulk estimates.
evidence.context: Red- and green-labelled complementary strands confined in sealed dimples. Each class fixes the counts of the two distinct partners.
fit: One red molecule and one green partner
evaluation: One red molecule and two green partners
One red molecule and three green partners
evidence.uncertainty: The figure shows error bars without tabulated uncertainties for individual bars. We calibrated on the one-partner class and evaluated the other classes from the same experiment. This cancels the common chamber volume. The authors fitted their confined dissociation constant using all classes. A separate calculation using bulk Kd depends appreciably on the volume estimate.
evidence.assessment: From one partner’s measured 0.48 bound probability, Cells predicted 0.649 and 0.735 with two and three partners. The figure gives about 0.64 and 0.67, respectively.

claims.title: A common catalyst factor preserves reversible rate ratios and equilibrium weights
claims.statement: On a positive reversible edge, catalysis preserves the forward-to-reverse rate ratio exactly when both rates receive the same multiplier. The transition-state law assigns a positive factor from the molecules common to both endpoints. The same equilibrium weights then balance the edge.
assumptions: The stabilizations are finite, dimensionless contact energies in kBT. A nonempty common membrane uses its molecular fractions. An empty common membrane has factor 1.
The rate-ratio identity refers to an available two-way transition. The equilibrium statement assumes the original rates and weights obey detailed balance on each edge.

numerical.result: Both directional multipliers agreed with the exact common-state value on 1,925 ordinary reversible edges. In an admitted two-molecule world with +20 kBT moving contacts and −20 kBT for the stationary molecule, float64 gives both rates as zero instead of 2.0611536224/s. The compiled run returns inert with a passing ledger. The equivalent constant-rate control fires at 0.3459699807 s on the same draw. With neutral movers and the same stationary contact, the clock runs with a 2.00 × 10⁻⁸ relative rate error.

biology.observable: Forward and reverse molecular transfer rates and an independently measured equilibrium partition under matched temperature and catalyst concentration.
biology.unit: s⁻¹ for each direction, dimensionless equilibrium partition
biology.finding: At 37 °C, cholesterol exchange between vesicles sped up about 57-fold with 1 mM β-cyclodextrin. Half-times were 195 ± 13 and about 3.4 minutes. A separate 0.5 mM equilibrium series gave a partition coefficient of 0.91 ± 0.06. Equal scaling of the two directional rates remains unmeasured. This transfer catalyst is in solution. [Leventis and Silvius, Figs. 1–2 and Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0006-3495(01)75873-0)

claims.title: Potassium rectification sets reversal, dissipation and a bound on slope conductance
claims.statement: On an open route the outward current changes sign at the Nernst potential and dissipates nonnegative heat. At fixed drive it scales with the square root of external concentration. The voltage derivative obeys the host’s upper bound even when the differential conductance is negative.
assumptions: The route carries a monovalent cation. Concentrations, absolute temperature, reference concentration and slope parameter are positive. The gain includes nonnegative area, availability and reference conductance. Reversal and sign require positive gain.

The derivative holds concentrations and route parameters fixed. The biological matched-drive comparison uses constant availability, rectification parameters and number of contributing channels across the potassium series.

numerical.result: The original stress case passed on main after the owner’s overflow-safe concentration factor landed. All three equivalent normalizations produced 0.5520533 pA and identical transfer and heat. The 360-state control panel passed. The original failure is recorded at the earlier engine revision.

biology.observable: Kir4.1 unitary current 60 mV below each measured reversal potential as external potassium changes.

evidence.locator: Panel C gives reversal, B(b) gives unitary currents and D fits the inward slope conductances from the same patch series.
evidence.context: Cloned rat Kir4.1 in HEK293T cell-attached patches at about 25 °C, three patches per concentration.
evaluation: 15, 21, 35 and 63 mM at a common −60 mV drive
evidence.uncertainty: Currents are approximate graph readings interpolated after reading the reversal for each series. Some reversal markers overlap. Per-point numerical uncertainties are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: At 15 mM external K the current magnitude fell less than the model predicted, as it did at the other three held-out concentrations. The model’s −59.67 mV shift in reversal agreed with the approximately −60 mV measured.

claims.title: The eight-state sodium–anion carrier shares a cycle flux and saturates with external substrate
claims.statement: Each edge of a steady ring carries the same net flux. For the declared two-sodium, one-anion cycle, exact detailed balance gives the host’s thermodynamic turnover and stall. For an active population at fixed voltage, sodium and internal substrate, the increase in inward current over its zero-substrate limit has the form A x / (K + x) for positive A and K.
assumptions: The carrier is at steady state on the single eight-edge ring with positive microscopic rates. Its forward and backward directions each bind the two sodium ions and the anion in the declared order. One net positive charge enters per forward cycle.

Equality with the thermodynamic rate assumes equal products of the base rate constants and a net electrical coefficient of −1 in the forward direction. A separate theorem retains the constant and voltage residuals for populations admitted within the engine’s detailed-balance tolerance.

The current comparison requires positive capacity and availability. The saturation result holds at fixed temperature, voltage, availability, all other activities and rate parameters. External substrate changes only its one forward binding rate. The reference current at zero substrate is the boundary value of the mass-action expression. The observed current is the measured steady current after subtracting its substrate-free baseline.

numerical.result: The capacity repair passed the original controls and all four extreme/zero capacity cases on NumPy and compiled CPU. At 10⁻³⁰² fmol/s the net readouts both gave 7.09691 × 10⁻³⁰⁵ fmol/s and reverse readouts gave 2.67423 × 10⁻³⁰⁷ fmol/s. The previous 100-fold diagnostic error remains recorded at its tested revision.

biology.observable: Baseline-subtracted steady current as external monocarboxylate concentration or clamped voltage changes. The dose series tests the functional form. A biological assignment for the individual transition rates and voltage coefficients remains open.
biology.unit: nA inward magnitude (propionate), µA signed current (lactate)
biology.finding: In an independent human SMCT oocyte series at −50 mV, the propionate half-saturation concentration was 128 ± 4 µM (SEM, n = 9). This pooled estimate constrains affinity. [Coady et al., Fig. 3A](https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.2004.063859)

evidence.locator: The data are the six filled symbols in the main propionate panel.
evidence.context: Human SLC5A8 in one representative Xenopus oocyte at −50 mV, 100 mM external sodium and pH 7.5. The inward current is measured relative to the substrate-free baseline.
evidence.uncertainty: The approximate graph-reading precision is ±5 nA. Per-point biological uncertainties and the measurement temperature are unspecified. The paper reports similar results from three additional oocytes.
evidence.assessment: Two calibration points gave K = 130 µM. At 250 µM the proven curve predicted 260 nA against 278 nA measured. At 2,500 µM it predicted 376 nA against 371 nA. The figure provides too little biological uncertainty for a population verdict.

evidence.locator: Subtract the substrate-free ibuprofen-sensitive trace from the 1 mM lactate trace at each negative voltage.
evidence.context: Human SMCT1 in a Xenopus oocyte, 96 mM external sodium, approximately 24 °C and pH 7.6.
excluded: Positive-voltage currents dominated by an anion leak
evidence.uncertainty: One representative experiment, approximate reading precision ±0.03 µA. Intracellular activities and kinetic parameters for this preparation are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: The inward current rose from about 0.68 to 1.40 µA in magnitude between −50 and −150 mV. Predicting that voltage dependence requires the transition kinetics.

evidence.locator: Filled symbols of the human propionate dose response at −50 mV.
evidence.context: Independent human SMCT oocyte series. The same two nominal calibration doses were used on this experiment’s current scale.
evidence.uncertainty: The caption gives n = 3 for the kinetic analysis. Pointwise biological errors and how the symbols aggregate the recordings are unspecified. Estimated figure precision is ±0.6 nA and about ±15 µM at low dose.
evidence.assessment: At nominal 200 µM, 22.6 nA was observed and 22.45 nA predicted. The two-point fit gave half-saturation of 140.2 µM and the paper reports 162 ± 26 µM. The original 250 µM residual remains untested in this independent series.

claims.title: Sodium coupling sets net charge and the stall voltage of an anion carrier
claims.statement: A forward cycle imports n sodium ions and one monovalent anion. The two source-side saturations and capacity scale the net rate. With n > 1 the carrier imports below its unique stall voltage. With n = 1 its rate is independent of voltage.
assumptions: Positive concentrations at N and P and a forward cycle from P to N. Both roles use the same standard state at their two ends. The engine admits n = 1, 2, 3 or 4. Capacity, availability and both saturations are positive in the active-stall theorem.

Equal-fraction external sodium and substrate changes assume fixed internal activities. Measured whole-cell voltage shifts yield the isolated shift ratio if both changes carry the same nonzero conductance weighting.

numerical.result: All 120 stages agreed with independent 60-digit free energies, saturation, rates and heat. The panel covered both orientations, all four sodium counts and twelve active stalls. The two-step tissue run gained exactly the lactate amount recorded as transported cycles and reported zero global charge error.

biology.observable: Charge per lactate, particles per charge and the ratio of voltage shifts with external sodium and substrate halving in human SMCT1.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 compares lactate uptake with current, and Fig. 2 compares volume with current. Fig. 4 uses both 96 to 48 mM and 48 to 24 mM sodium steps, each paired with substrate halving.
evidence.context: Human SMCT1 in Xenopus oocytes. The Cells declaration cites this study for the two-sodium coupling.
evaluation: Lactate and propionate zero-current shift ratios
evidence.uncertainty: The reported charge uncertainty was ±0.07 across five batch slopes. The volume/current and shift ratios are reported as mean ± SE.
evidence.assessment: The two-sodium carrier also predicted 3 osmolytes per charge versus 3.1 ± 0.1 measured. It predicted a shift ratio of 2 for both sodium halvings. The experimental means were 2.2 ± 0.2 for lactate and 2.3 ± 0.3 for propionate. Absolute stall and Hill kinetics remain open.

evidence.locator: Human series, square symbols. The x axis is integrated charge and the y axis is radiolactate uptake.
evidence.context: An independent laboratory measured human SMCT in Xenopus oocytes. The coupling was fixed from the Coady study.
fit: Coupling n = 2 from Coady et al.
evaluation: Four distinguishable human lactate uptake/current pairs
evidence.uncertainty: Approximate figure readings rounded to 5 pmol. Individual experimental uncertainties are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: Measured net charge exceeded the prediction at all four human points by approximately 65–85 pmol. At 370 pmol lactate, Cells predicted 370 pmol net charge and the figure gives about 450 pmol.

claims.title: Potassium–anion cotransport follows the concentration products in a closed pair
claims.statement: The active 1:1 route moves outward when the inside concentration product is larger, stalls at equality and dissipates nonnegative heat. Equal amounts of the two ions move together. With equal fixed volumes, the exact trajectory approaches equilibrium monotonically. An explicit ARS(2,2,2) step can move in the opposite direction if it is too large for the closed pair.
assumptions: Potassium has valence +1 and its partner −1. Concentrations and temperature are positive. The rate scale is capacity times availability times the exponential volume factor. Strict direction and stall require a positive scale.

The closed-pair trajectory assumes one route, equal fixed finite volumes, constant availability and no other transfers. The explicit stage calculation uses the ARS(2,2,2) order condition. All formal operations are in real arithmetic.

numerical.result: After the product-ratio fix, both extreme concentration cases gave finite affinity and heat matching the independent references. At 2⁻⁵¹⁰ mM outside they were 1,836,599.47 J/mol and 4,701.69 pJ/s. All 27 ordinary controls passed. With fixed and moving water, the original 10 ms step was refused and the 32- and 64-step refinements passed. The previous failed cases remain in the earlier checkpoints.

biology.observable: External cation concentration at reversal normalized by internal potassium, plotted against the inside/outside chloride ratio.
biology.finding: Rabbit red cells gave an outward K:Cl flux ratio of 1.12 ± 0.26 (SD, five preparations), consistent with the model’s 1:1 stoichiometry. The investigators measured rubidium as a potassium tracer and calibrated its relative flux. [Jennings and Adame, Fig. 5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11502559/)

evidence.locator: Figures 5–7 estimate the reversal point from zero net flux. Figure 8 fits normalized reversal against the chloride ratio.
evidence.context: Low-potassium sheep red cells with pH and volume clamped. The assay compared outward K and inward Rb flux after chloride-minus-nitrate subtraction.
evidence.uncertainty: Eight points contributed to the normal-magnesium fit and ten to the low-magnesium fit. The paper gives correlations of 0.912 and 0.976. It gives no uncertainty for either slope.
evidence.assessment: The ideal product rule predicts a slope of 1. The measured slopes were 1.12 at normal magnesium and 1.08 at low magnesium. Rubidium substitutes for external potassium. The volume dependence of net flux remains open.

claims.title: Water potential sets flow, heat and osmometric equilibrium
claims.statement: Water moves down the hydrostatic-minus-osmotic pressure difference. At frozen solute amounts this potential is the volume derivative of free energy after unit conversion. Dissipated heat is nonnegative. An outward potassium–anion cycle increases the outward water drive by moving two osmoles across the membrane.
assumptions: All volumes and temperature are positive. Osmoles are ideal, elastic pressure is linear in volume, and mobility and stiffness are nonnegative. Each held bath has fixed pressure and concentrations.
